extracted.intended_audience: Employers, immigration attorneys, HR professionals, labor advocates, and stakeholders involved in H-1B/H-1B1/E-3/PERM prevailing wage determinations and related rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Regulatory guidance and proposed rulemaking criteria for computing prevailing wages used in H-1B, H-1B1, E-3, and PERM labor certification programs, including allowable wage sources, percentile-based wage levels, classification procedures, and statutory rationale. Intended to guide how Departments/NPWC determine wage levels and how employers must comply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice to employees
rubrics_metrics.description: Employer must provide notice to its employees in the affected occupational classification by posting the notice in a conspicuous location at the worksite or through other means such as electronic notification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a procedural requirement tied to LCAs (labor condition applications); see cited authority. The page treats conspicuous posting or electronic notification as acceptable methods to provide notice to affected employees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevailing wage determination as of LCA filing
rubrics_metrics.description: The prevailing wage must be determined as of the time the LCA is filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timing is critical: employers must use the prevailing wage applicable at filing rather than some other date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitted sources for prevailing wage
rubrics_metrics.description: An employer may base the prevailing wage on: (1) an applicable collective bargaining agreement (CBA) negotiated at arm's length that contains a wage rate for the occupation; (2) a Prevailing Wage Determination (PWD) from OFLC; (3) a wage determination under the Davis-Bacon Act or Service Contract Act; (4) an independent authoritative source such as a private wage survey that satisfies 20 CFR 655.731(b)(3)(iii)(B); or (5) another legitimate source (e.g., industry compensation study) that satisfies 20 CFR 655.731(b)(3)(iii)(C).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employers are not required to obtain an OFLC PWD; multiple legitimate sources are enumerated, but private or industry sources must meet regulatory criteria in 20 CFR 655.731(b)(3)(iii). The rule cites the regulatory provisions that define acceptability.

rubrics_metrics.name: LCA filing window (six-month rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: An employer may not file an LCA more than six months prior to their selected start date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This limits how far in advance employers may lock in a prevailing wage via LCA filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: LCA certification timeframe
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless the Secretary finds the LCA is incomplete or obviously inaccurate, the Secretary must certify it within seven working days of its filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seven working days is the statutory/administrative certification target unless deficiencies are present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-certification filing requirement (Form I-129)
rubrics_metrics.description: Once an employer receives a certified LCA, it must file Form I-129, Petition for a Nonimmigrant Worker, with USCIS if seeking classification of the alien as an H-1B worker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certification of the LCA is a prerequisite to filing the I-129 for H-1B classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: USCIS adjudication checks on petitions
rubrics_metrics.description: During adjudication USCIS determines whether the petition is supported by a certified LCA that properly corresponds to the petition, whether the employer's position qualifies as a specialty occupation, and whether the alien is qualified for the position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: USCIS evaluates correspondence of LCA to petition and substantive eligibility (specialty-occupation requirements and beneficiary qualifications) as part of I-129 adjudication.

rubrics_metrics.name: OEWS as primary federal wage data source
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department has long used the BLS Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics (OEWS) survey as the primary wage source for establishing skill-based prevailing wage determinations; OEWS produces employment and straight-time gross wage estimates across SOC codes with annual May reference date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OEWS is the largest continuous federal wage survey, covering over 1.1 million establishments over a 3-year sample and providing geographic and occupational granularity not available from other sources; no commenter identified a more suitable dataset in the 2021 RFI.

rubrics_metrics.name: OEWS wage definition and exclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: OEWS wages are defined as straight-time, gross pay (including piece rates) but exclude premium pay like overtime, shift differentials, non-production or year-end bonuses; OEWS excludes self-employed, owners/partners in unincorporated firms, household workers, and unpaid family workers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using OEWS, prevailing wages reflect straight-time gross pay only; limitations of coverage (excluded worker types and pay forms) must be considered in methodology.

rubrics_metrics.name: OEWS two-component structure (employment and wage)
rubrics_metrics.description: The OEWS survey consists of an employment component (estimates of full- and part-time jobs across occupations/geographies) and a wage component (estimates of straight-time gross pay for employees in an occupation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both components inform labor-market and wage distribution understanding; the wage component is what the Department incorporated into prevailing wage guidance in 1997.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical OEWS-to-wage-level conversion (two-tier then four-tier)
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically the Department used a two-tier conversion of OEWS data (Level I = mean of lowest paid one-third ≈17th percentile; Level II = mean of upper two-thirds ≈67th percentile) and in 2005 expanded to a four-tier system mapping to approximately the 17th, 34th, 50th, and 67th percentiles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The four-tier structure was created to approximate wages commensurate with experience/education/supervision when OEWS did not provide explicit skill-level differentiators within SOC codes; mathematical formulas were applied to produce intermediate levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory requirement for four commensurate wage levels
rubrics_metrics.description: When a government survey is used to determine the prevailing wage, the survey must provide at least four wage levels commensurate with experience, education, and level of supervision (INA §1182(p)(4)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statutory mandate underpins the four-tier wage structure; levels must meaningfully differentiate by experience/education/supervision.

rubrics_metrics.name: NPWC job classification and wage-level determination process
rubrics_metrics.description: The NPWC (National Prevailing Wage Center) examines the nature of the job offer, area of intended employment, and job duties; uses the SOC taxonomy and sources like O*Net to classify the occupation and determine the appropriate wage level by comparing the job description, title, and requirements (education, training, experience, skills, knowledge, tasks) to those normally required for the occupation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each job opportunity begins at Level I and may progress to higher levels (II–IV) based on the comparison; the process is stepwise and fact-based using authoritative occupational sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: 2020 IFR and subsequent percentile adjustments (litigation context)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 2020 Interim Final Rule (IFR) revised computation methodology: Level I as mean of fifth decile and Level IV as mean of upper decile, shifting wage levels approximately to the 45th, 62nd, 78th, and 95th percentiles; litigation followed and the Final Rule later adjusted Level I and IV percentiles (e.g., to 35th and 90th in the Final Rule), but courts vacated/remanded aspects and rulemaking was delayed/reexamined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The IFR and Final Rule chronicle the Department's attempts to increase wage floors, the legal challenges alleging inadequate notice-and-comment or arbitrary action, and the Department's responsive revisions; litigation history affected implementation timing and scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: NPRM proposed percentile increases (current proposal)
rubrics_metrics.description: This NPRM proposes to increase prevailing wage floors (OEWS-based) to: Wage Level I from ~17th to 34th percentile; Level II from ~34th to 52nd; Level III from ~50th to 70th; and Level IV from ~67th to 88th percentile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department cites that prior methodology set wages too low and failed to account adequately for experience/education/supervision as required by the INA; the proposal aims to reduce incentives to hire lower-paid alien workers and prevent adverse effects on U.S. workers' wages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy rationale: protect U.S. workers and align with INA
rubrics_metrics.description: Prevailing wage determinations serve as a safeguard to ensure employment of alien workers does not adversely affect wages and working conditions of U.S. workers; statute requires employers pay the greater of the actual wage or the prevailing wage (100% of wage determined).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department grounds its authority in INA §§1182(a)(5)(A), 1182(n), 1182(t), and §1182(p)(4) to revise methodology consistent with protecting domestic labor markets; changes are justified by statutory duty and evidence of wage suppression under prior levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on H-1B occupations and need for cross-program consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department focuses analysis on the H-1B program because it comprises the largest share of workers covered by the wage structure and because adverse effects are most acute where concentrations of such workers exist; revisions to H-1B wage methodology also implicate H-1B1, E-3, and PERM due to unified use of the four-tier structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintaining consistency across programs prevents employers from exploiting divergent wage structures to circumvent higher wages; emphasis on occupations with large H-1B employment is appropriate given program overlap and pathways to permanent residence.

rubrics_metrics.name: OEWS limitations for specialty-occupation alignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Because OEWS was not specifically designed to reflect the INA's 'specialty occupation' requirement, OEWS data for a given occupation may not perfectly align with H-1B statutory qualifications (highly specialized knowledge, specific-degree baseline), which affects how OEWS should be integrated into prevailing wage determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department recognizes OEWS as the best available dataset but notes methodological adjustments are needed to ensure wage levels better reflect wages of U.S. workers most similarly employed to H-1B beneficiaries (e.g., EB-2 and higher-skilled EB-3 comparators).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and qualification standards for specialty occupations
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'specialty occupation' requires theoretical and practical application of highly specialized knowledge and attainment of a bachelor's or higher degree in the specific specialty (or equivalent); having 'any bachelor's degree' is insufficient—degree/personnel requirements must be specialized to the job.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These statutory and regulatory definitions constrain which jobs qualify as specialty occupations and therefore shape determinations about appropriate wage levels and comparisons to similarly employed U.S. workers; qualification pathways include specific-degree, state licensure, or equivalent experience plus recognition through progressively responsible positions.
